title: J.C. Higgenbotham as a trombonist and man
summary: Higgenbotham was one of the best trombonists Holmes heard, instinctive rather than schooled, easy to work with and fond of a drink.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: What about J.C. Higgenbotham? What can you tell me about him?
It's nothin' much I can tell you about him...except that he was a helluva trombone player. And he did his work, and he could play. He loved to blow his horn,

and he loved to take a little taste. And he didn't bother nobody. He was not the violent type or anything like that. He didn't care what anybody did, as long as he could sit up there and play his horn. And you couldn't find too much for him to play. He loved to blow. And he could blow...and now and then he'd take a little taste. Sometimes he'd take a little taste too much. But I guess that happens to you.
But Higgy was great to work with. He was great. Yeah, him and Red worked together for years, after they got out of Russell's band. Yeah, they worked together for years.
Well, would you rate Higgy as one of the best trombonists around at the time?
One of the best I ever heard in my life.

He was one of the best I ever heard. I mean, just for a plain, every-day trombone player, yes, he was one of the best I ever heard in my life. He was fine. And I don't think... Higgy I know didn't have no whole lot of musical education. He was no Juilliard man or anything like that. He was a plain, ordinary musician. But he could play. Hell of an instinct. Yeah, a good man. One of the best I ever played with. Very creative. And easy to get along with. Very easy to get along with. A very nice person.
